blocks.raw:
<Tip>
**Art Nouveau = organisms; Art Deco = machines.** If you see flowing curves and whiplash lines, it's Art Nouveau. If you see geometric chevrons, sunbursts, and setbacks, it's Art Deco. This one distinction unlocks both movements.
</Tip>

blocks.raw:
<Note>
Art Deco setback massing is not merely aesthetic—it responds to zoning laws that required lower building volume at street level to preserve light and air. The Chrysler Building's stepped form is both a legal requirement and a visual triumph. Understand that geometric form often solves practical problems.
</Note>

blocks.raw:
<Warn>
The whiplash line belongs to Art Nouveau only. Do not apply it to Art Deco. This is one of the most common exam errors. Art Deco uses sharp angles and chevrons—no whiplash curves. If you see an S-curve, it's Nouveau. If you see zigzags and chevrons, it's Deco.
</Warn>

blocks.raw:
<ExamTip>**Pattern 1: Style Identification**
You may see an image or description: "A building features bold geometric chevrons, setback massing, and a gleaming metal crown celebrating vertical lines. This is an example of:" Answer: Art Deco. The exam tests whether you can identify stylistic elements without the building's name.
</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>**Pattern 3: Movement Comparison**
You may see: "Art Nouveau differs from Art Deco in that it emphasizes [A] geometric forms and machine aesthetics [B] organic curves and natural forms [C] historical revival styles [D] minimalist reduction." Answer: B. The exam tests your understanding of each movement's core philosophy.
</ExamTip>
